Question: Can agents commission work from other agents: task negotiation, capability matching, SLA agreement, delivery, and acceptance?
Response: Yes. Within a single domain, work specialisation happens via skills inside the domain Hosted Agent with MAF workflow graph edges as the coordination substrate — no inter-agent protocol required, no network hops, one Entra identity, one audit trail. Across domains (Hiring → Finance) and with external off-platform agents (partner candidate agents, supplier agents, jurisdictional authorities), A2A protocol governs work commissioning. An agent executor can: (1) Discover available agents via AgentCards in APIM (capability matching). (2) Send task requests via A2A JSON-RPC (task negotiation). (3) Agree on SLA parameters encoded in the task request. (4) Receive results via A2A task completion. (5) Evaluate results via Foundry Evaluators, a MAF validator executor, or in-session quality checks (acceptance). MAF's stable multi-agent patterns (sequential, concurrent, handoff, group chat, Magentic-One) express cross-domain coordination directly in the workflow graph; DF coordinates phase boundaries with timer escalation. All A2A traffic governed by APIM with per-skill tool allow-list enforcement. Non-revocable actions from A2A invocations (e.g. outbound A2A to external agent, results-affecting writes) fall under the Git-committed non-revocable ops catalogue with dual-control (two Entra identities in two operator groups) for high-risk. See response §18 for the Skills-vs-Multi-Agent rationale.
Key Technologies: A2A protocol (cross-domain/off-platform), APIM (agent discovery + per-skill allow-list + JWT claim validation), Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) multi-agent patterns, skill-based intra-domain specialisation, Azure Durable Functions (coordination + dual-control enforcement), Foundry Evaluators (acceptance), non-revocable ops catalogue

Question: Do agents maintain trust scores with other agents based on reliability, quality, and response time? Are scores observable and auditable?
Response: Agent performance metrics serve as a foundation for reputation scoring. OTEL telemetry and APIM metrics track per-skill: completion rates (reliability), Foundry Evaluator quality scores (quality), and response latency (response time). These metrics are observable on the Control Plane and auditable via Application Insights. A Fleet Manager skill could compose these metrics into a reputation score per skill per domain (skills are the specialisation unit within a domain Hosted Agent; reputation tracked at the skill level within the domain's governance boundary) — but this is not a pre-built reputation system. It would require custom skill development to: aggregate metrics into a composite score, track scores over time, and factor scores into routing decisions (prefer higher-reputation skills for high-value tasks). The underlying data is available; the reputation logic would be custom.
Key Technologies: OTEL metrics, APIM metrics, Foundry Evaluators, Fleet Manager (custom reputation skill)

Question: How does the platform resolve contention when multiple agents compete for the same resource? Describe deadlock detection for circular dependencies.
Response: Resource contention is managed at multiple levels. (1) APIM rate limiting: per-skill per-domain, per-tool rate limits prevent a single skill from monopolising an external API. The per-skill tool allow-list (compiled into APIM policy fragment) also prevents a skill from calling tools outside its declared capability set — rejected at the gateway. Requests exceeding limits are queued or rejected with retry-after headers. (2) Durable Functions + MAF graph orchestration: DF defines phase-level execution order across the workflow envelope; within each phase a MAF workflow graph uses Pregel BSP execution where each superstep waits for the prior step to complete before advancing — making parallel access to shared resources inspectable and contention-free by construction. (3) Cosmos DB concurrency: optimistic concurrency with ETags prevents write conflicts on shared state. Conflict resolution via conditional updates. (4) Deadlock prevention: the Durable Functions orchestration graph is a DAG (directed acyclic graph) — circular dependencies are prevented by design. Timer escalation ensures no phase waits indefinitely. If a resource is unavailable (locked by another process), the retry policy handles backoff and the Fleet Manager alerts on sustained contention.
Key Technologies: APIM rate limiting, Azure Durable Functions DAG (no circular dependencies), Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) v1.0 (Pregel BSP execution), Cosmos DB optimistic concurrency, timer escalation
